---
title: "What do engineers do with computation, and why is it awesome?"
subtitle: "MCEN 1030 · Introduction to Engineering Computing"
---

Welcome to MCEN 1030: Introduction to Engineering Computing, taught by Professor Jeremy Koch in the Fall 2026 semester.

We are trying a new approach to this class this semester. When I took this course (circa Fall 2006... oof), the big challenge for students was to figure out how to use fundamental programming ideas — loops, conditional statements, indexing — to achieve an engineering task. My professors gave us very clean problem statements so that we could focus on writing the code. This is no longer the process of programming! AI (artificial intelligence) and specifically LLMs (large language models) have proven they are extremely capable of writing code based on a prompt (natural language instructions), and so they solve well-specified problems almost instantaneously.
::: {.column-margin}
We can argue if LLMs are actually a form of artificial "intelligence" — we'll talk in this class about how they are actually just statistical word-guessers.
:::

For better or worse, it seems LLMs are here to stay, and so we will learn how to integrate them into our computing workflow. Most engineers are not manually typing in `for i in items:` anymore, they are writing prompts that include phrases "...iterate through the items in that list..." and having ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, or Co-Pilot write the code. 
::: {.column-margin}
If they are using a "local LLM", one that is not run on the cloud (and thus one that is not sending out company secrets), they might be using Qwen, Gemma, Deepseek, or another open-source model. 
:::

That doesn't mean it is not important to understand code. We are not going to treat LLM-generated code as a "black box". We we learn why LLMs are not 100% trustworthy and that will motivate us to learn about the concepts, the meanings of errors, etc., so that we can troubleshoot and improve upon code. And, after all, if you end up using an LLM result in your job and an engine explodes, you won't be able to blame ChatGPT — it's your fault! So we better make sure we understand what is going on in the code.
::: {.column-margin}
We can't look inside a "black box" to see what is going on.
:::
  



## The big idea

The process of creating computational tools looks roughly like this:

```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 700 150" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:700px; width:100%; height:auto;">
  <title>The computational pipeline</title>
  <desc>Five boxes in a row: Idea, Specification, Production, Verification, Use, connected by arrows. A curved arrow labeled Adaptation loops from Use back to Specification.</desc>
  <defs>
    <marker id="arr" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="6" refX="8" refY="3" orient="auto">
      <path d="M0,0 L8,3 L0,6 z" fill="#2b2b2b"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>
  <g font-family="sans-serif" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">
    <rect x="5"   y="40" width="90"  height="40" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#2b2b2b" stroke-width="1.5"/>
    <text x="50"  y="65">Idea</text>
    <rect x="135" y="40" width="120" height="40" rx="6" fill="#fbf7ec" stroke="#8a6d1f" stroke-width="2.5"/>
    <text x="195" y="65">Specification</text>
    <rect x="295" y="40" width="110" height="40" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#2b2b2b" stroke-width="1.5"/>
    <text x="350" y="65">Production</text>
    <rect x="445" y="40" width="110" height="40" rx="6" fill="#fbf7ec" stroke="#8a6d1f" stroke-width="2.5"/>
    <text x="500" y="65">Verification</text>
    <rect x="595" y="40" width="90"  height="40" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#2b2b2b" stroke-width="1.5"/>
    <text x="640" y="65">Use</text>
    <line x1="95"  y1="60" x2="133" y2="60" stroke="#2b2b2b" stroke-width="1.5" marker-end="url(#arr)"/>
    <line x1="255" y1="60" x2="293" y2="60" stroke="#2b2b2b" stroke-width="1.5" marker-end="url(#arr)"/>
    <line x1="405" y1="60" x2="443" y2="60" stroke="#2b2b2b" stroke-width="1.5" marker-end="url(#arr)"/>
    <line x1="555" y1="60" x2="593" y2="60" stroke="#2b2b2b" stroke-width="1.5" marker-end="url(#arr)"/>
    <path d="M 640 82 Q 640 130 420 130 Q 195 130 195 84" fill="none" stroke="#2b2b2b" stroke-width="1.5" marker-end="url(#arr)"/>
    <text x="420" y="122" font-style="italic" font-size="13">Adaptation</text>
  </g>
</svg>
```

For decades, **Production** — actually thinking about the code structure and typing the code — was the bottleneck, so intro courses like this one spent nearly all their time on it. That bottleneck is gone: AI tools produce working code from a good description in seconds. The new bottlenecks are the two highlighted boxes:

**Specification** means describing the problem precisely: the inputs and outputs, what has to happen in the middle, what to do at the edges. If you cannot articulate the problem, no tool — human or AI — can solve it for you.

**Verification** means refusing to trust a black box: sanity-checking results against hand estimates, testing edge cases, knowing the ways a program (or a model, or an AI) goes wrong.

You will still read and run and modify plenty of code in this course — you can't verify what you can't read. But you will be graded on whether you can *think computationally*: frame a problem, direct the tools, and audit the results. That is what engineers are actually hired to do.

## How a week works

**Before class**, you read one lesson on this site (30–45 minutes) — and the lessons are *runnable*: most code on these pages executes right in your browser, editable, no installation, no setup. (When you want more than the browser — Colab, or Python on your own machine — the [getting going page](info/installing.qmd) has instructions.) No videos to watch, no Canvas quiz. Instead, every lesson ends with a **Bring to class** box: one question you answer *on paper, committed, before you arrive*.

**Class opens with that question.** You'll vote on it, argue with your table, and vote again. If you didn't do the reading, you will know it, and so will your table. That's the whole accountability system, and it works better than a quiz because you can't outsource an argument.

**Mondays are optional.** All semester, one weekly optional session: [Base Camp](info/basecamp.qmd) early (the beginner on-ramp, plus checkpoint dress rehearsals), [Side Quests](info/sidequests.qmd) later (build a tiny language model, 3D-print a parameter sweep, and more). No grades attached, just help and getting to know each other.

**Four Tuesdays open with a checkpoint** (weeks 4, 6, 8, 10): twenty minutes, individual, on paper, no AI — where the convergent standards get demonstrated for real, with earlier items re-offered so a rough week is always repairable. Everything about how that feeds your grade is on the [grading page](info/grading.qmd).

**The rest of class is work at the tables.** Early in the semester that's mostly short problems with right answers. Later it shifts toward open-ended problems where every table's AI-assisted solution comes out *different*, and the interesting question becomes *why*.


**Homework** are mostly about real mechanical engineering and will be formatted to include four steps: specify, annotate, verify, report. (The code is not what's graded). The [homework page](homework/index.qmd) explains the format.

## AI policy

You are **expected** to use AI tools in this course. You are also **completely responsible** for everything they produce for you. Every assignment asks you to show your specification, annotate the generated code, and demonstrate your verification. The final exam asks you to explain what is actually going on inside a project *you* produced.

## Grading

This course uses **standards-based grading**: a list of specific skills ([the standards](info/standards.qmd)), each marked *Met* or *Not Yet*, plus **engagement credits** for committed preparation and in-class work — credited for good faith and not for correctness. There is no partial credit, no point-scrounging, and no penalty for struggling early: you can demonstrate a standard later when it naturally reappears, and your grade is where you *end up*, not where you started. The full mechanics, including a grade table and worked examples, are on the [grading page](info/grading.qmd).
